positions.stance: Argues that independent technical safety boards and targeted compute subsidies can insulate academic and smaller labs from compliance overhead.
Contends that comprehensive behavioral red-teaming requires proprietary infrastructure controlled exclusively by dominant cloud providers, turning compliance into corporate capture.

positions.stance: Prioritizes catastrophic risk mitigation and structural verification over deployment speed, arguing that unverified failures cause irreversible harm.
Prioritizes rapid access to automated diagnostic tools and therapeutic development, arguing that precautionary gating imposes a direct human toll.

verdicts.conflict: Whether behavioral audits and pre-deployment capability evaluations can be administered fairly without entrenching the market power of major cloud providers who own the required testing infrastructure.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic and supporting claims provide a concrete mechanism of failure regarding grant review boards and proprietary hardware dependencies. The safetyist position relies on theoretical exemptions that lack empirical proof of neutralizing corporate capture.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Publicly verifiable audits run on neutral infrastructure that consistently onboard independent developers without major cloud provider intermediation would flip this verdict.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the risks of unmonitored capability scaling outweigh the economic and medical costs imposed by regulatory delays.
verdicts.rationale: The debate weighs incommensurable metrics: catastrophic existential risk versus immediate, quantifiable economic and therapeutic delay. Neither framework offers an objective conversion rate between irreversible low-probability tail risks and near-term utility.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical consensus on the probability distribution of catastrophic model failures versus the verifiable public health opportunity cost of delayed model deployment would break the tie.
